title: Hedge Funds Navigate a Volatile Week
summary: LPL Research examines hedge fund performance, portfolio de-risking, and crowding during a volatile week for equity markets.
body_markdown:
# Hedge Funds Face Stress Test


[Michael McClain](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/michael-mcclain.html) | Alternative Investment Research Analyst and Due Diligence


Last Updated: November 11, 2026


Hedge funds encountered a difficult but revealing market environment over the past week. A sharp decline in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks, rising stock correlations, and rapid reductions in portfolio risk created a challenging backdrop for several strategies. Yet results varied considerably. Equity-oriented managers generally struggled, while lower-beta, market-neutral, and selected defensive approaches provided better protection. That dispersion offers an important reminder; “hedge fund” describes an investment structure, not a single strategy. A long/short equity fund, a trend following manager, and a market-neutral strategy can respond very differently to the same event. Understanding the role each strategy is intended to play may therefore be more useful than judging the entire category by one volatile week.


## A Difficult Week for Risk Assets


For the week ending November 6, broad risk assets came under pressure as investors reassessed the outlook for artificial intelligence spending, interest rates, and policy. Large growth stocks were hit particularly hard, with the Russell 1000 Large Growth index falling 4.8%, while the information technology sector declined 8.2%. The market’s internal behavior was as important as the headline index returns. Stocks increasingly moved together during the sell-off, reducing the diversification that long/short managers normally seek from individual stock selection and paired positions. Crowded technology holdings were also unwound as hedge funds reduced gross exposure, which is the combined value of their long and short positions, and net exposure, the difference between those positions. This was not simply a case of the stock market declining and hedge funds participating proportionally; it was also a positioning and factor shock. Managers concentrated in growth, momentum, semiconductors, and other artificial intelligence beneficiaries faced pressure from their long holdings and from a broader rush to reduce leverage.


## Gross Exposure Was Already Moving Lower


Prime-brokerage data suggest that the reduction in hedge fund risk did not begin last week. According to data attributed to Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, cumulative hedge fund gross flows had declined approximately 8% from their June peak, representing the largest sustained stretch of long/short equity de-risking in more than 15 years. Although hedge funds briefly became net buyers of U.S. equities during the week of October 23 through October 29, the activity appeared to be driven primarily by short covering rather than by managers adding new long positions. Short covering can produce strong market rallies, but it does not necessarily signal greater confidence in the underlying outlook. A manager who buys back an index short is reducing downside risk mitigation. That is different from identifying an attractive company and establishing a new long-term position in pursuit of an upside. Selling longs raised liquidity and lowered gross exposure.


## Crowding Amplified the Decline


Crowding was central to the week’s performance. AI-related stocks had become widely owned across hedge funds and traditional long-only portfolios. When a popular trade reverses, multiple investors may attempt to reduce the same positions simultaneously. Reported prime-brokerage flows indicated that hedge funds have become underweight the broad artificial intelligence trade for the first time since early 2023. Long sales outpaced the establishment of new short positions by roughly 3.5 to one. That pattern indicates liquidation rather than a broad expression of a negative fundamental view. Managers were primarily selling positions they already owned, rather than aggressively betting that technology stocks would continue to decline.


## Strategy Results Varied Widely


- Equity long/short managers appear to have been among the most affected, with technology-focused, quantitative equity, and some multi-strategy funds also central to the technology-related liquidation.
- Managers with high net exposure, concentrated technology books, or heavy momentum positions generally faced a more difficult environment compared to diversified managers operating with lower net exposure. Market-neutral and low-beta factor approaches held up better, although higher stock correlations made traditional relative-value trades more difficult.
- Managed futures strategies were also caught by abrupt reversals. Many trend-following programs entered November short bonds, went long energy andlong the U.S. dollar, and positioned for selected equity trends. Several of these moves reversed at nearly the same time. These outcomes reinforce that managed futures are not designed to anticipate market turning points. They generally perform best when price trends persist and may struggle when several established trends reverse before portfolio models have time to adjust.


## What Investors Should Consider


- The first indicator to monitor is whether gross exposure stabilizes. Continued reductions would suggest that managers remain focused on capital preservation rather than on identifying new opportunities.
- Second, investors should distinguish between short covering and genuine long buying. A rally driven by covering can be powerful but may fade if fundamental investors do not participate.
- Third, watch stock correlations and market breadth. Persistently high correlations would indicate that portfolio level risk reduction is still overwhelming company-specific fundamentals. An improvement in breadth would provide a better environment for long/short stock selection.
- Finally, monitor whether AI exposure is being rebuilt gradually or whether managers quickly return to the same concentrated positions. A slower rebuilding process accompanied by broader participation would represent a healthier backdrop than renewed crowding in a small group of technology leaders.


## LPL Research Main Takeaway


LPL Research’s main takeaway is that one volatile week should not determine a strategic hedge fund allocation, but it can reveal what risks investors own. Recent performance showed that some equity hedge funds carried more technology, momentum, and market sensitivity than their strategy labels may have implied. At the same time, market-neutral and lower-beta approaches provided better defense, while managed futures struggled with a rapid cross-asset reversal. The reduction in gross and net exposure may eventually create a healthier opportunity set because positioning is less extended, and weaker hands have been forced to sell. However, low exposure alone is not a buy signal. Stability in volatility, broader market participation, and evidence of fundamental long buying would provide more convincing confirmation. For investors, the most important question is not simply whether a hedge fund gained or lost money, it's whether the result was consistent with the job the strategy was selected to perform.
